I'm Suhani Balaji, a second-year B.Tech (Hons.) student at RV University. My major is Cybersecurity, and my minor is Business Administration.

I code, I enjoy breaking problems down, and cybersecurity is the field I want to build my career in. My courses so far include C programming, data structures, operating systems, databases, embedded systems, IoT, computer networks and cybersecurity. Outside class, I serve as Assistant Secretary of ChipTech, our technical club.

I chose a business minor to understand how companies actually work. Security decisions are business decisions too, and I want to speak both languages when I join the corporate world, or if I start a company of my own one day.

My goal: to become a cybersecurity analyst at a multinational fintech company.

What I offer recruiters: strong technical foundations, coding and analytical skills, and the confidence to lead and speak up.

Why I chose this path

I wanted to protect systems, and I also wanted to understand the companies that depend on them. A major in cybersecurity gives me the first. A minor in business administration gives me the second. Together they prepare me to work in a company, or to start my own.

Coursework · Semester 3 · Minor

SB1022 Business Communication

Course overview

Course code: SB1022 · Title: Business Communication

Semester 3 · Minors, School of Business, RV University · Ability Enhancement Course (NEP) · 3 credits (3:0:0) · 15 sessions of 3 hours, 45 hours in total · Faculty: Prof. TM Srinath

Objectives

  • Provide an in-depth understanding of the nuances of communication.
  • Help recognise the role of non-verbal communication in workplace settings.
  • Offer guidance to develop clarity and precision in business writing.
  • Support the skills for effective report writing and documentation.
  • Strengthen oral communication through discussions and presentations.

Submitted work

Group 3 · CIE 4 · 22 slides

ReWear: a pitch for circular fashion

Group 3 pitched ReWear, a marketplace where people can buy, sell and rent pre-loved fashion. We covered the problem of full wardrobes and low trust in resale, an AI-verified trust layer, the rent and sell journeys, the unit economics and our ask to investors.

My contribution. I worked with my six teammates in Group 3 to prepare the pitch and present it to the class.

What I learned. A pitch is a report told as a story: problem, solution, why now, numbers, then the ask. I also saw that trust sells. ReWear depends on verification, which is the same promise I want to deliver in cybersecurity.

Modules, learnings and class videos

Pick a module to see what I learned and the videos we watched, each with my one-line takeaway.

Module 1: Communication, Types and Barriers

My key learnings

  • Communication is a process, not a one-time event. It is complete only when the receiver understands the message. Example: in class we followed a message from thought to encoding to decoding.
  • Every message has six elements: communicators, the message, noise, feedback, context and channel. Example: when I use a technical term that a listener doesn't know, that term becomes noise.
  • Communication has a purpose: to inform, persuade or motivate. Example: Steve Jobs sold the benefit, "1,000 songs in your pocket", instead of the spec.
  • Non-verbal cues carry a large share of the meaning. Example: Jobs used pauses, an open stance and eye contact so that his ideas felt as strong as his words.
  • Strong communication shapes careers. Employers rank it as a top skill when hiring graduates. Example: as a cybersecurity student, I will need to explain technical risks to people who don't code.

Videos from class

  • Steve Jobs: a case study in presentation (video 1)He explains one idea at a time and lets a simple slide back it up.
  • Steve Jobs: a case study in presentation (video 2)The pauses and the plain words are planned and practised, not accidental.
  • Mr. Bean, The ExamA whole story of exam panic is told with no dialogue, only face and body.
  • Non-verbal communication: guess what the bird is sayingI guessed the meaning from tone and movement alone, which is how non-verbal cues work.
  • Himansee Katragadda: Navarasa, 9 variations of emotionsNine emotions from one face showed me how much expression can say without words.
  • Mitch Lomazov: Bridging the Generational Gap in the WorkplaceDifferent generations prefer different channels, so I should ask instead of assuming.
  • Workplace Communication: Enhancing Connections Through Active ListeningListening means giving full attention and checking my understanding before I answer.

Module 2: Types of Non-Verbal Communication

My key learnings

  • When words and body language disagree, people tend to trust the body. Example: in class, a manager says "I'm not upset" with crossed arms and no eye contact, and the team believes the body, not the sentence.
  • There are seven types of non-verbal communication: kinesics, oculesics, proxemics, haptics, paralanguage, chronemics, and artifacts and appearance. Example: for my self-projection video, I planned my posture, eye contact with the camera lens, framing, voice and clothing.
  • Mehrabian's 7-38-55 figures are a narrow finding about feelings, not a law of all communication. Example: the Module 1 slides quoted percentages for facial expression and tone. Module 2 taught me to treat them as an illustration, not an exact rule.
  • Digital body language is real. Tone, timing and format carry meaning in text too. Example: a very short chat reply can sound cold, so I now read my message back before sending it.

Videos from class

  • Amy Cuddy: Your Body Language May Shape Who You AreStanding tall before a presentation changes how confident I feel going in.
  • Joe Navarro: The Power of Nonverbal CommunicationComfort and discomfort show in the body first, so I should notice them in others and in myself.
  • Erica Dhawan: Digital Body LanguageOnline, reply time and punctuation do the job that tone and gesture do in person.
  • Optional: Celeste Headlee: 10 Ways to Have a Better ConversationA good conversation needs full attention and real curiosity about the other person.

Module 3: Business Writing: Emails, Messages and Memo

My key learnings

  • The 7 Cs make writing work: clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous. Example: I used them to check every page of this website.
  • Use the direct approach for routine messages and good news, and the indirect approach for bad news. The indirect approach places a buffer and reasons before the bad news. Example: a rejection email should explain before it refuses.
  • BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) saves the reader's time. Example: I now state my main request in the first line of an email.
  • AI can draft, but I must check and stay in charge. A prompt formula like P-A-C-T (Persona, Audience, Context, Task) helps, but the final message must be accurate and my own. Example: this website's rules let me use AI for ideas, but the words must be mine.

Videos from class

  • Sal Khan: How AI Could Save (Not Destroy) EducationAI is most useful as a tutor that guides my thinking, not one that does the work for me.
  • Victoria Turk: How to Write an Email (No, Really)A clear subject line and a short, polite message respect the reader's time.
  • Guy Katz: How to Write an Email That Will Always Be AnsweredAn email gets answered when the request is specific and easy to reply to.
  • Jason Fried: Why Work Doesn't Happen at WorkInterruptions break focus, so a written update is often better than a meeting.

Module 4: Business Reports

My key learnings

  • A report is organised, factual and written for a reader who has to make a decision. It should be accurate, objective, structured and actionable. Example: our ReWear pitch put the unit economics on one slide so an investor could judge the model quickly.
  • The executive summary is written last but read first, and conclusions are different from recommendations. Example: in class we practised writing an action title and a short executive summary from a small table of data.
  • Data storytelling follows a setup, insight and resolution arc. Example: we worked with real UPI data and turned numbers into a story.
  • AI can structure a summary, but I must verify every number. Example: in the raw-data-to-summary lab, the AI draft still needed a human check.

Videos from class

  • Ben Wellington: Making Data Mean More Through StorytellingNumbers become memorable when they are tied to one simple, relatable story.
  • Hans Rosling: The Best Stats You've Ever SeenA moving chart with a clear narrator can change what people believe about the world.
  • Bonus: David McCandless: The Beauty of Data VisualizationGood visual design lets patterns appear that a table would hide.

Module 5: Debates and Discussions; Business Presentations

My key learnings

  • The Rule of Three makes ideas easy to remember. Structures like PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explain, Link) and PREP (Point, Reason, Example, Point) keep answers clear. Example: my video script uses three strengths.
  • A pitch follows an order the listener can trust: problem, solution, why now, numbers, then the ask. Example: our ReWear pitch opens with "The Problem" and closes with the ask of ₹8 crore for 10%.
  • Personal branding means honestly managing how others see my professional identity. Example: my LinkedIn profile, this website and my video should all show the same person.
  • Web readers scan in an F-pattern, so the headline, hero section and call to action matter most. Example: my Home page puts my headline and a "Contact me about internships" button at the top.

Videos from class

  • Julian Treasure: How to Speak So That People Want to ListenMy voice has tools (pace, pitch, volume and silence) and I should use them on purpose.
  • Chris Anderson: TED's Secret to Great Public SpeakingEvery talk should plant one idea worth sharing in the listener's mind.
  • Sandra Long: LinkedIn's Community, A Superpower Hiding in Plain SightLinkedIn is a community to take part in, not only a profile to fill in.
  • Lyn Cacha: How to Build Your Powerful Personal BrandA personal brand is what people consistently experience from me, so it has to be honest.

My professional vocabulary

  • NoiseWhen I explain a cybersecurity idea using jargon, the jargon becomes noise for someone who doesn't code.
  • Active listeningBefore I reply in a group project, I try to paraphrase what my teammate said to check that I understood.
  • Digital body languageA reply that arrives after two days, or has no greeting, says something even if I didn't mean it to.
  • BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front)I now put my main request in the first line of an email so the reader doesn't have to hunt for it.
  • Call to actionEvery page of my website ends with a clear call to action, such as "Contact me about internships".

Blog

10 November 2026

Why a cybersecurity student is learning to write emails

I chose cybersecurity because I like understanding how systems work and how they break. So when my minor in business administration brought me to a Business Communication course, I wondered how it would help me.

Then I thought about what a cybersecurity analyst really does. Finding a vulnerability is only half the job. The other half is explaining it to someone who doesn't speak code: a manager who has to approve the budget, or a team that has to change how it works. If they don't understand the message, the fix doesn't happen.

That's where business communication comes in. A few ideas from this course already stand out to me:

  • Know your audience. A technical team and a company director need very different explanations of the same problem.
  • Be clear and concise. A short, well-structured message gets read, and a long one gets skipped.
  • Body language speaks too. Posture, eye contact and tone shape how people receive a message, even on a video call.

I used to think technical skill was enough. I now believe it's only the starting point, and the people who go furthest can also explain their ideas, persuade others and lead. That's what I want to be: a cybersecurity analyst who protects a company and can also explain why it matters.

This blog is where I'll keep track of what I learn, one post at a time.
